utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Theresa McHenry for the Prosecution along with Mr. Turone and Mr. Huber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Eugene O'Sullivan. I appear on behalf of Mr. Delalic. My colleague and lead counsel, Ms. Residovic, will not be here this morning. She will be back at 2.30 when we call our next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Tomislav Kuzmanovic along with a legal assistant, Nico Duric, here on behalf of defendant, Mr. Mucic. I would like to advise the court that tomorrow Mr. Duric will be present, I will not be present and he will be here on our behalf, on Mr. Mucic's behalf. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic attorney from Sarajevo, defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. My colleague, Mr. Tom Moran, will not be present for the next two weeks due to family business.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Cynthia McMurray for Esad Landzo and my colleague, Ms. Nancy Boler, will appear at 2.30 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I haven't been announced, I am Michael Greaves and I am here to assist Mr. Karabdic in one matter today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We'll start this morning with Delic's motion for a binding order. Has the Prosecution anything to say about it? We have not seen your own response to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's right Your Honour. It was only recently filed. Our response will be very short and I am happy to give it orally. I will note for the record that there's no indication that the Defence has attempted to get these documents without a binding order or that the FRY has been provided notification of their request, such that their position may be ascertained. With respect to the position of the office of the Prosecutor, regarding the request, we defer to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the motion now. Let's hear the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's in respect to this matter that I have been asked to assist Mr. Moran and Mr. Karabdic today. Your Honour, of course having sat on the appeal concerning the issuing of subpoenas and binding orders to state officials and individuals acting in their own private capacity, we'll be well familiar with the decision that was issued in October of last year and so I needn't go in at any great length, to that decision. Suffice it to say that the conclusions that the Tribunal, the Appeal Chamber came to on that occasion were these: The Tribunal is empowered to issue binding orders and/or requests to states and those states are obliged to comply with them. The tribunal may not address binding orders to state officials acting in their official capacity. As far as individuals are concerned, there are extensive powers to summon subpoena and address other requests or binding orders to that. Set out in the motion are a series of categories of documents, each of which, in my respectful submission to Your Honour, is not only relevant but highly relevant to the proceedings before this tribunal. Can I take first of all at page 1 of Mr. Moran's document, Item A-1. Your Honour will recall there has been some evidence about the time at which pressure was placed upon the Yugoslav government. As a result of which it appears that orders were issued to extract from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the then called JNA. Your Honour, paragraph A-1, in our respectful submission, adequately identifies a category, probably quite a small category, a category of documents, the nature of which is highly relevant in our respectful submission to the issue of international armed conflict, which is one of the matters squarely before this Tribunal. Secondly, paragraph A-2. Again, that is an issue which goes squarely to two matters before the Tribunal. Firstly, the issue of international armed conflict; and secondly, the issue of nationality. Again, in my respectful submission, it is sufficiently identified, that the category of documents which are sought and again, in my submission, easily identifiable by the government to whom that would be directed. Thirdly, at paragraph A-3, which is at the top of page 2, Your Honour. Again, all reports in possession of the government to the federal republic of Yugoslavia, received from the JNA or other entity, indicating the extent of compliance with the orders that were given under paragraph 1 and 2 above. Again, in my submission, sufficiently identifiable. Again, probably quite a small category of documents which ought to be easily retrievable from the appropriate place. Paragraph 4, again, an issue that goes to the very heart of the question of international armed conflict. The matter which was extensively discussed in the matter in judgement in the Tadic case. The possession of those documents would enlighten, greatly, this Tribunal in our respectful submission. Again, a category, a class of documents sufficiently identified in our respectful submission to enable swift retrieval by the federal republic of Yugoslavia. I turn now to paragraph B, which is at the bottom of there. Your Honour, there is a report and I have in my possession that report, so that if further identification is required of such documents, it can be given. Those are items which go to an issue of impeachment that only Mr. Moran has identified. Paragraph B-1 to 4 set out a series of items that are sought. Plainly this was a report prepared by the federal republic of Yugoslavia. One anticipates that it is easily identifiable, provided the files comprising that report have been maintained. Each of those documents ought to be readily identifiable. Paragraph 4 seeks, actively, the assistance of the federal republic to identify the identity and location of those witnesses. Your Honour, paragraph B-5. It's quite some time ago now, but I am sure Your Honours remember, the lady who is identified there. She plainly appeared on television in Belgrade some two months before or the the month before she gave evidence last year. A copy of that is in the possession of the defence. However, in order to properly to prove it, it is sought in the terms that are set out in paragraph B-5. A means of proving it properly is sought. It may, however, be, of course, that my learned friend for the Prosecution might agree to admit that such an event took place and that would circumvent the need for such an order in that case. Your Honour, those are the documents. In my submission, they are sufficiently identifiable and that of course was one of the matters that Your Honour and your brother judges in doing the appeal in the Blaskic subpoena decision were obviously anxious about, the question of sufficient identification of documents. In my respectful submission, the documents are relevant, have probative value or would have probative value and are documents that would be of great assistance to this Tribunal to see. In my respectful submission, Your Honour has the power, the documents are identified and it would be proper to grant the orders that are sought by my friend Mr. Moran and Mr. Karabdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Some of my problems are whether you have made any efforts to obtain these documents and from your motion I think all of them are public documents and they do not belong to any classified category as far as your memorandum here issues. You have not indicated what efforts you have made to take them and have them refused. I don't see why you should start with a binding order when no effort has been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As I understand it, no significant effort has been made to recover these documents from the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They're public documents, especially the reports of the committee, will be a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The report, of course, is a public document. But the documents, upon which the report was based, are not. It's the documents upon which the report is based that are sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The documents related to the withdrawal of the JNA, you have not indicated within any category which you cannot obtain ordinarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just using one's common sense, I suspect they're a class of documents that there will be some reluctance to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, let's not go on that assumption until there is a refusal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, give me a moment, please. Your Honour, one problem my friend Mr. Karabdic is faced is of course there exists as between his country and the FRY, at present, no diplomatic relations, so that presents some difficulties to him in making the request on an official basis to the government of the FRY. I'm sorry, I interrupted Your Honour and I do apologise and I did follow up on what Your Honour is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is not a question between two governments. It's between counsel and the authority in possession of these documents. It is counsel who should make the approach and then show to the Trial Chamber that he has been refused, when, in fact, they show the documents are there. Now one of these documents are related to impeachment and you indicate certain witnesses under light. It's fairly difficult to know how that is related to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is one matter -- I haven't had an opportunity to speak to Mr. Moran as to the precise nature of that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't you think you're really not properly equipped to move the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, that may be right, but, Your Honour, what I suggest is this: That the best way to deal with this matter is perhaps to adjourn it without coming to a conclusion upon it, so that at least one further step can be done before drawing it back to Your Honour's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think so, until we have a firm refusal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think that would be kind if Your Honour would do that and that would assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. So the motion is adjourned. We wouldn't strike it out, but ordinarily one would have struck it out, but we'll adjourn it. We now turn to the application in respect of protective measures for DB.1. Have you any observations?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we defer to the court in that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Also like the earlier motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise for not having had the opportunity to read it yesterday, given our short response. It would have been more efficient had I been able to tell you yesterday, but we defer to the court entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What precisely are the protective measures you are seeking? In regard to the witnesses of the Prosecution, their names will appear and that sort --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- and you also want their face to be sort of covered or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct. You'll note, Your Honours, the ten items, the standard items from the protection of that nature, the minimum protection of identity and disclosure to the public or to the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's all?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, well, there should be no objection to that, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No objection to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The application is granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To the extent that the face not be shown and his identity not be indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, we have another motion from Hazim Delic about the designation of an expert witness. Mr. Greaves, are you aware of that too, the designation of expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: (Microphone not on).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It doesn't work as well as the one down the other end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Karabdic prepared to take this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there has been a misunderstanding; however, let me take on this motion. Hazim Delic requests that an expert be assigned and the name of this expert witness is Carl U. Kent. Mr. Kent is an experienced investigator who has been involved in over 2,000 investigations, and he has appeared in over 600 court cases as an expert witness. On the basis of the transcript of these proceedings, he is going to testify on whether the injuries to which the Prosecution witnesses testified were possible and whether the consequences which the witnesses have mentioned were possible and were durable. This expert witness is going to say whether the kinds of blows and the number of blows that the witnesses alleged to have sustained, for instance, with the baseball bat and similar instruments would be possible. He is also going to investigate other types of injuries to which witnesses had testified, and I think that he is going to be able to shed light on the veracity of the witnesses testimonies. We do not have independent corroboration for these testimonies. We do not have medical reports which would have been issued immediately following these alleged injuries. We only are relying on witness statements and their testimonies but we do need an expert witness which is what we are requesting and we ask that our motion be granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might assist Mr. Karabdic for a moment, I do have personal experience with the expert that they have requested. He was my investigator on one murder case in 1992 and he was the Prosecution's investigator on a capital murder case that I represented in 1996. I can speak that he has vast experience and he is an excellent investigator and probably has as much forensic experience, as far as testifying about injuries, as any person I know, if that may assist the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if the Defence were trying to hire this person as an investigator, the Prosecution would not object. But if they are trying to call him as an expert about injuries, we certainly would object for reasons including that he is an investigator, not a medical expert; even looking at the material supplied, there's no indication that he can assist Your Honours in questions of expertise dealing with injuries. Even assuming a medical expert would be able to do that based on reports, it would have to be a medical expert, not a police investigator. We would be objecting to the calling of this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He's not a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, he's not. He's a sergeant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Only a forensic one, forensic medicine --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't have his CV in front of me because I don't have that document. But if I recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Surely you've relied on his evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have and I've had hundreds of cases since then. I do believe that when he left the Prosecutor's office in Harris County, he was a homicide detective before that, if I remember correctly, before he went into investigative work which, I believe, would qualify him as a homicide detective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We want someone who has specialised in the forensic aspect of the medical profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A forensic person who specialised in the forensic department of the medical profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I can't testify that he does represent that part of the profession. I'm not quite sure. I do know that he has vast experience in murder cases and injuries; and from his experience, since there are no medical reports to rely upon, I think that Mr. Delic is asking that he be allowed to testify from his experience in injury cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Has he made any investigation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically in this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not qualified to respond. My guess is that he has not travelled to Bosnia. I don't believe he has even travelled to The Hague yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: He would speak in theory about injuries, without being a medical doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe he would be speaking hypothetically and in theory, and I don't believe that he has done anything except review the daily records and transcripts of this case. I'm just assisting from what I believe is my experience with this expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: So he hasn't examined any of the alleged victims?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't imagine he has. Only Mr. Karabdic can answer those questions, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you sure he has examined any of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was just going to offer my assistance as far as I'm able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I don't know how he can be put forward as an expert. If you can give us good reasons why he should be accepted as an expert, one can then consider the business for which he has been called, as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, enclosed with our proposal is his resume and his working career. It is stated here that he took part in investigations and reconstructions of numerous cases of murder and inflicting of serious bodily injuries. In this case, in our case, I believe that he would be of significant assistance to us. He hasn't studied the transcript so far, but we would request him to do so and to provide an opinion on that. This has been articulated in our request, in our motion, and we do believe that he would be able to help us in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has defined who an expert is, and it doesn't appear he comes within the scope of those persons who we have accepted as experts, in any particular field as such, because I don't see how he could be accepted as an expert. An expert in what? That is what concerns us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise at this moment. Has Your Honour actually seen the curriculum vitae of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I direct Your Honours' attention to, first of all, paragraph 1. That is considerably more, I think, the homicides and most --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It says detective.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, I was going to go on to the next paragraph where he has given expert evidence in more than 600 criminal trials. That, I think, is extremely extensive expertise that's involved in giving evidence of that kind in so many trials. He plainly, as far as the authorities in his home state are concerned, is recognised as an expert in such investigations. Your Honour, it's not just doctors who can give evidence about the effect that hitting somebody 500 times with a baseball bat, in a period of five hours, can give. Police officers who have been involved in an investigation of this kind of incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't you think a doctor, an anatomist would be in a better position to give us a good opinion with regard to the effect of 500 blows over a period of five hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But that doesn't preclude a police officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He should have some knowledge of the human body.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- from testifying about the effect of such injuries and such assaults.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Surely you can find forensic experts who can tell us probably more qualitatively as regards to the effect of such a large number of blows over such a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, the point is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We're not holding investigations here. I'm sure he's a very good investigator. I'm sure he's a very good detective, but we're concerned with the effect of such a large number of blows on a person over such a short period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I just draw Your Honours' attention to page 2 of the man's CV?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Does Your Honours see in about the middle page under his education?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Education, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours will see that he has had extensive training, particularly, for example, in the issue of blood splattering and so on. Those are the sorts of issues that are dealt with by forensic medical witnesses as well. So he has, in my submission, extensive education and expertise in that area. That, no doubt, is why the state of Texas uses him as an expert witness. Your Honours, in my submission, there is also this: One of the issues that comes from having lawyers from all over the world is this: We all have our own experts who we know and trust, and my learned friend Mr. Moran knows and trusts this police officer or ex-police officer. It is important, in my submission, as part of the process of defending against charges of this kind, that counsel have the opportunity to use those witnesses who they believe to be experts who fall, in my submission, within the category of expert witness, in whom they have confidence. It may very well be that Mr. Moran would have to find somebody that he doesn't know if he had to find a forensic medical expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. If you read it carefully, he is coming to give evidence on his opinion of what others have said. This is what he is coming to do, and that is the expertise he is giving to us. If it is one of a more common sense deduction of what has happened, otherwise, everybody can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He comes from Houston, this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It looks like he's a gentleman of Houston, born and bred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm sure this sort of forensic person -- Houston is a very big city. You can certainly get one from there who specialises in forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My submission is that he does fall within the category that Your Honours have identified as being expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: One may have some lurking doubt. That is the only expert in this field. When we have an expert about whom -- when we have a lurking doubt that he is really not an expert. The first question the Prosecution would ask in cross-examination is, "Have you studied medicine?"

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, it's a matter for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And once he says "No," then some sort of doubt is created in one's mind, whether he's really competent to express opinion on matters which he is not specialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That goes to the issue of weight. It doesn't go to the issue of whether or not at the present time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why produce a witness about whose opinion there cannot be any lurking doubt?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, there it is. The application is made. In my submission, he, as we stand here at the present time, falls properly within the category of expert. I would respectfully invite Your Honours to say that this is a man who can give proper evidence to this court. If I can say so from my own experience, he's far more experienced than any police officer that I've come across in England, but then we don't have quite so many murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, that's comparing him with police officers. Who would then be accepted as experts in this particular area, of whether certain injury was sufficient to cause that or not? That is the issue, whether the type of beating claimed would be sufficient to kill the victim. Now, what he is coming to tell us is that it would not be sufficient to result in that. That's not somebody who is properly trained and accredited for the purposes of ascertaining or satisfying that that has occurred, not somebody who could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My submission would be that both men can do an equal job and do it from a different perspective. The fact that there may be someone who will do it better doesn't necessarily preclude my learned friend calling someone in whom he has confidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: A doctor is a better person that is accepted as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Think over your positions. Maybe you can get a medical expert. Just think it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps we can again return to this matter as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I just might add one bit for the record, I do have to say that as a criminal defence attorney, I have used him as an expert in Stephen Jones case in 1992, and also he was quite devastating when he testified for the Prosecution in the capital murder case of Hilton Crawford in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Was he testifying for the Prosecution or the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He was testifying for the Prosecution against me. I was defending in 1996 and his testimony in recreating the murder scene was quite devastating, and it was trial by jury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A murder scene and a detective is one thing, but tell us about the effect on a human body of such a large number of blows with a baseball bat in such a short period is really a medical question. I've just suggested to Mr. Greaves to think it over. We're not disposing of it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I do understand with the indication that the court would find some doubt in this expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I don't say that we will; maybe. There's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wanted to state that in my jurisdiction, he has been an expert witness many, many times. If that's of any assistance, then fine. If not, then it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Frankly, speaking for myself, I concede that any jurisdiction can accept its own definition of expertise and rely on that. But here since the rationale of what he is coming to say is that certain conduct can result in that or not in that. That area of expertise has been preserved to medically trained persons who we all accept can satisfy that and not those who have not been authorised to do that. What he's saying is what any intelligent person can say, that if given so many blows can result in -- we can all guess, but our own guesses might not be as informed as that of a medically trained person. This is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I respect the decisions and the comments of the court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have not yet given any decision. We just asked him to reconsider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: To think about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is all we have. Now, this is all we have for this morning. We will return at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 10.42 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. This afternoon, I think we are at the mercy of Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I fear for two minutes, you get to be at my mercy as well. If Your Honours give me two moments just to mention one matter, please. Just before lunch yesterday, I wasn't present. Your Honour indicated that you would communicate a decision as to when one particular motion would be heard. Could I gently jog Your Honour's memory so that you tell us when you want to deal with that matter on concerning judicial independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I indicated yesterday, in the first place, I would say the application was wrong in the order in which it was made. If you looked at it, I mentioned it, I said if you looked at Rule 15, the application should be made to the presiding judge. It is not an application intended for argument in open court unless there are differences. So it's not a question for which -- the application was not made to the presiding judge, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's expressed as being to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's not what Rule 15 said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could I inquire because there are two possible definitions of presiding judge. I assume by the words "presiding judge", that is to Your Honour as presiding judge of this Trial Chamber, rather than at the present, the Tribunal as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The president is not a presiding judge except he has a Trial Chamber in which he presides. If you make an application to the presiding judge, it is not an application to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would Your Honour like us to re-address it solely to Your Honour so that we can actually get it going?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I would have it in any event dealt with it in accordance with the rules. I definitely will deal with it, irrespective of the fact that it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As a matter of formality, would you like us to resubmit it to you personally as opposed to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a better way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The rules must be obeyed and that is why they are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sorry, for taking Your Honours' time. Would you think it very rude of me if I withdrew, I have other things to attend to this afternoon outside the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I grant you leave, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So now you're showing mercy to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Residovic. We will start with your first witness. Would you kindly invite the witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him take the oath first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can now take your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I start, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. EMIR DELALIC

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Emir Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, thank you for accepting the invitation of the Defence and thank you for coming here despite the fact that you had to travel overnight to appear before this Tribunal as a witness. Before I begin with my questions, let me draw your attention to a technical matter. You and I speak the same language and it would be very easy for us to proceed with these questions and answers, however, you must bear in mind that our conversation must enter into the transcript and after I ask my question, after I have finished my question, would you please listen to the interpretation coming from the earphones that are on your desk. When you hear that the interpretation has finished, then you can answer my question. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, could you tell the court when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Prozor on the 18th of March, 1962. Prozor is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your educational background, what schools did you go to and where did you complete your education and what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed elementary education in Prozor and secondary school for mechanics, I completed in Konjic and my profession is mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 1990, I lived and I worked in Prozor, as of 1990 I have been living in Austria, that is in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you still live in Austria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, tell me, is Zejnil Delalic related to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's your father's brother, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you when the war began on the 6th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Austria.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you become involved in Austria in the humanitarian work for the defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, like most other citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, do you know whether your uncle, at one point in time, before the war, whether he went to Konjic and, if he did so, why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that at the beginning of April or maybe end of March, he went to attend the funeral of my other uncle, together with my two other uncles from Austria, and he stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These two other uncles of yours, did they come back to Vienna after the funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether your Uncle Zejnil Delalic stayed in Konjic in order to help the defence in a way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most probably that was the reason why he stayed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were in Vienna and you told us that two of your other uncles had come back to Vienna, could you tell us whether they also participated in the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- well, we all try to find ways to help Bosnia-Herzegovina. We attempted to collect some money or something else that might be useful for the defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names of these two uncles of yours, Zejnil's brothers who were in Vienna at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefik and Dzemal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dzemal also took part, participated in the defence forces and, if he did, could you tell us in what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he used to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina from time to time. He would usually spend 20 days in Bosnia-Herzegovina and then he would come back to Vienna and stay 20 days in Vienna and this went on for a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about Sefik, the other brother, did he participate in the defence as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. At the beginning of June, he went there and he stayed there until the end of July, approximately. According to what he told me, he was very active in the establishment of the military police of the then territorial defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Zejnil Delalic have a brother in Zagreb and, if he did, what is his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did have a brother in Zagreb, his name was Vejsil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he also participate in collecting the humanitarian aid, logistical aid for the defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. During that period, the roads to Bosnia and Herzegovina were blocked by Serbs and he used his channels, his links to transfer certain amounts of money or some other types of assistance, like food or clothes and this is why we used him to send the humanitarian aid there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, at one point in time during 1992, did you, yourself, go to Bosnia-Herzegovina and did you also take part in the defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you tell me when and how, I would like to ask you whether your closest family was living in Konjic at that time and I am referring to your father, your brothers and whether they were also members of the defence forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father and my brother were in Konjic at the time and they were members of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did you come to Bosnia and Herzegovina and where -- in which area did you stay while you were taking part in the defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my Uncle Sefik returned, I went to Bosnia-Herzegovina at the end of July, beginning of August, and I went to Konjic and Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your visit to Konjic, was it in any way related to the transport of the humanitarian assistance that had been collected by our citizens in Austria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had some money and some other goods, like cigarettes, a couple of radio stations, small portable radio stations and some drinks for my Uncle Zejnil.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Konjic, were you a civilian or did you become a soldier at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a couple of days, maybe three or four days, I could not find a uniform, so I was a civilian at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you came to Konjic, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first went to Zejnil's house hoping to find him there, to give him the cigarettes and some wine, but he was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to a farm that belongs to my aunt, a couple of kilometres away from Sarajevo, where my father was staying. A couple of kilometres towards Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that it happened at the beginning of August, could you tell me whether you learned, at some point in time, where Zejnil was and what function he held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned the whereabouts of Zejnil from my father and he told me he was appointed some kind of commander of a TG-1. That was the abbreviation. And he was at Igman and at the position not far from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, what was your father involved with when you arrived in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, my father had a warehouse, he was actually working at the Celebici barracks. This is what I learned a couple of days later when we went there together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just answered my following question. I wanted to know whether during that time, while you were in Konjic, whether you visited the barracks in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us now, who did you go with to the barracks and how did you get there? Did you go there by car, on foot or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went there by car. We took a white jeep to get there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any specific work to attend to in Celebici when you went there on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one day after, or maybe two days after my arrival, Irfan brought some batteries, empty batteries and we wanted to go to Celebici to fill them up because that was the only possibility to do that. Apparently there was some kind of station for recharging batteries.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was any one with you at that time in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were three of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your father, yourself and?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you got to the barracks, was that your first visit to the barrack, was that the first time that you actually entered the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first time that I went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where that station for recharging batteries was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was located next to the command or some kind of administration building. It was on the left hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So did you manage to finish your work as soon as you got there. That is, did you eventually recharge these batteries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did, but not as soon as we got there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got to the gate, my father asked one of the guards where the key was and how he could recharge his batteries. And the guard told us to go to Hazim Delic and he told us that he had the key because he often had to recharge batteries on his vehicle and on some other vehicles as well. So we stopped near the station, but Hazim was not there at that moment. And there was another guard standing there and my father asked him about Hazim and the guard told us that he had just gone to have lunch and that we could find him in front of one of the hangars. So we continued to the hangars and at the entrance of one of the hangars, I saw Hazim Delic. And my father told me that this was Hazim. He was standing, or maybe he was approaching the entrance to the hangar and we parked not far for him, maybe 5 or 6 metres away from him and we went towards him and he had already entered the hangar and I was very close to the threshold and at that moment, my father called him. He said something like Hazim, we need the key. And then all of a sudden we heard one or two shots and we were surprised and we were frightened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment when you heard the shot, at that moment did you have the key that you were looking for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at that moment. I think that it somehow happened at the same time. He was giving me the key, he was throwing it at me and I realised that the rifle fired, it was some kind of automatic rifle. And when my father said that we needed the key, so he was about to throw it to us, and I didn't quite see it, but I heard maybe one or two shots in the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I ran away, I ran outside. I was probably at the entrance, but I didn't know what was happening, so I simply ran away. Hazim wanted to see what it was all about and we went back to the vehicle and we drove back to the station for recharging batteries.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, while you were still at the barracks, did you learn what had happened? What this shot was all about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it took us awhile to recharge the batteries and one of the guards said that someone had been wounded. Apparently the bullet ricocheted from the ceiling and that person who happened to be there, at the ambulance, that he was injured and that he was given, apparently, he was given first aid immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Delalic, were you wearing uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not have an uniform at that time. I had a pair of jeans on and a T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that you came to the door of the hangar, were you able to see anybody inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could only make out figures of persons, but outside it was very sunny and it was dark inside. It was very hot, but I could not make out anyone's face.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But were you in a position where somebody from inside the hangar could see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that I could have been seen by a number of people. Because I believed that I was either at the threshold or I had stepped inside one or two steps and that's where I was startled by this shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you had recharged your batteries and learned that a person had been injured in there and was given medical aid, did you leave immediately afterwards, the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We first went to the warehouse where my father worked, and I found a uniform and I found a rifle and I took those.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, do you know Mr. Pavo Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you see Mr. Pavo Mucic at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were present when the bullet was discharged and later you heard from the guards what had happened, can you tell in your own judgement, was this sort of an accidental discharge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, I'm 100 per cent sure that this was accidental because he was carrying the rifle like this on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, did you come back to the Celebici barracks at any other point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Later I came back at least five or six additional times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go on each of these subsequent occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the warehouse where my father worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at any of these occasions when you went to the Celebici barracks, see any of the persons who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some five or six days after I came from Vienna, I went in the same way, the jeep, because I had trouble clearing checkpoints with my Austrian car with Austrian registration plates; so I used the jeep because I had no problems with that. On this occasion, I went to pick up my father who had stayed at the Celebici barracks longer than usual. So I went over there and I helped him load up some crates and we started out. As we were going from the warehouse to the gate, about some 20 to 30 metres away from me, I saw two men who were filleting a sheep, skinning it, on some railroad tracks. My father told me to slow down, actually, to stop there, to pull over so that he could greet this person. His name was Smajo, nickname Kurecan. He was a butcher. Kurecan came over slowly and greeted us in a sort of local way, and my father asked him, "Why are you doing this? What kind of feast are you preparing there?" And he said that this was a sheep -- Smajo and Kurecan usually had these sheep in the compound, but he said that he had to kill this sheep. My father said, "How can you give a knife to a Chetnik there, a weapon?" And he said his name was, I think, Zeleni which means green. He was an older man and he said that he was a fellow butcher who had a butcher shop in Bradina. They were good friends. They were colleagues, that he had arranged with Guska for him to be released and so that he would most probably already be released.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, did you know this person of whom you're talking now before? I'm not talking about Smajo but about this butcher from Bradina; did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know him, but Smajo said that he was his colleague, that he was from Bradina and that his name was Zeleni.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, you just mentioned another name, the name of Guska. Did you know at that time when this conversation took place in 1992; did you know who Guska was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew. I knew who Guska was. I knew this man from before the war and he was a vet in the town of Konjic. I knew him on a private basis because he used to come to Prozor either on business or privately. I know that during the elections in Konjic town, he was elected or appointed, I should say, the chief of the MUP station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at that time or subsequently meet any of the staff of people who worked in that administration building in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is when I first saw Pavo. It was in the compound. We were approaching the administration building because my father needed to bring back the key to the warehouse. This took no longer than half a minute to a minute, and my father walked out with Pavo and greeted him. I greeted him too and I knew him from before. He said, "Here's Pavo. See, now he works here. He no longer digs manholes and trenches in Austria like before," and then we greeted each other and I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said several times now that you drove a white jeep. Whose jeep was it and do you know who drove it in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The jeep belonged to my Uncle Zejnil. There was a white jeep and a green jeep. I drove this jeep while I was there. I don't know if I was there for a month, a month and ten, twenty days. Also my father, my brother, Irfan, just about anybody who needed it, drove it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else in your family have a white jeep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My Uncle Sefik also had one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have this jeep in Austria or in Konjic while he was engaged in the defence efforts in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had bought that jeep in Austria but he drove it down to Konjic and he kept it with him while he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, you can probably answer the following question: Is your family, the family Delalic, a large family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We know that one of your uncles died just before the war, on the eve of war. How many brothers were alive, including your Uncle Zejnil, in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, there were five of them alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were all of them in Konjic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them with exception of Vejsil who worked and lived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name Dzafer Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was my oldest uncle who died, I believe, in 1984 or '85.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, if somebody said, in this court, that they saw your Uncle Dzafer Delalic in the Celebici compound, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That this is not true and that he couldn't have been there even in theory because he had died some six or seven years before the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, did your uncles bear any family resemblance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who looked the closest to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefik and Zejnil looked alike the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are they all sort of strongly built?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody is sort of built like myself and my Uncle Zejnil.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the Celebici barracks with your Uncle Zejnil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He and I never went in there together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him during your stay in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first saw him sometime in the latter part of August before the swearing in for the TO members of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of your testimony, you said that for awhile you were in Konjic town and then later you went to Prozor. During this period, did you, in a way, join the Territorial Defence of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived in Prozor, I reported to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence. They knew that I was not going to stay long in Prozor, but I offered to do whatever I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know in 1992 the commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence in Prozor on a personal basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know his name? Do you know his first and last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence in Prozor was Muharem Sabic. And from other people from Prozor, I learned that before the war he was a career military man, so he was very welcome in the territorial staff, and it was also Smajo Rujic who was also from Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Prozor, could you learn from the people in the headquarters what the relations were between the Territorial Defence headquarters and the HVO in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How is he a competent witness on this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Probably not for the overall relations, but for the period of time when he was there, he could know because he was both from Prozor and he had contacts with the municipal staff. So I'm limiting my questioning of him to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can say. If you know anything, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my judgement, the relations were good because the army, that is, the TO of Prozor at that time and the HVO together manned the front-lines towards Kupres where the Chetniks were. As far as the military cooperation is concerned, that was all right, but there was tension around. This had something to do with the school system, but I did not try to find out more about that. But in terms of their holding together, the front-lines at Kupres, that was fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My next question now is redundant because I wanted to ask you whether during your stay there, there was any kind of armed conflict between these two components of the army, and you already said that the relations were good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was none.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Prozor, did you learn that your Uncle Zejnil Delalic had some command authority over the staff with which you were briefly involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody mentioned him as their potential commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, at some point in time, in 1992, the HVO attacked the forces of the Territorial Defence in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I returned to Austria, sometime in early September, I think it was around 10 September, the situation was regular in Prozor. But about ten days later, I was surprised to hear on Austrian television that the units of the HVO had attacked the town of Prozor. I was surprised and shocked to hear that because my mother had remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Except for the news on Austrian television, did you have any other information about your family suffering certain damage during that attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I later learned through some people that my house was one of the first ones to be hit by a shell from a tank, and it was partially burned. The majority of Muslim houses were Prozor were damaged, and about 95 per cent of the Muslim population was driven out, and a part of the Muslim population managed to organise some kind of resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, you told us about your experiences. I would just like you to look at certain documents offered by the Prosecution, and I would like to show the witness certain documents. I think it's Prosecution Exhibit 1. I think these are some photographs of the Celebici compound. I'm being alerted to the transcript; I'm not sure. Let me ask you to look at the photographs, and if you should see a photograph that you recognise, please put that photograph on the ELMO and explain anything that relates to that photograph, that is, if any of the events which you related took place in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about the gate itself. It may not be that interesting. I can show in this photograph where the batteries were recharged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a number next to that photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is number 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put that photograph on the ELMO, and then you also have a pointer somewhere near you, if you can use it to point to the structure or room where these batteries were recharged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to, for the transcript, say that the witness pointed to a structure where the batteries were recharged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can show on photograph number 33; this is the hangar where the accidental shooting occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put it on the ELMO and can you point to where it is? Can the photograph please be displayed on the ELMO? Yes, thank you. Can you now please point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me whether the door to the hangar, when you were there; was the door open or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door was open.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, the witness has identified this area. Is there another photograph in this album, which is the Prosecutor's Exhibit, which you can recognise as a place which you went to during your visit to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the photograph of the warehouse where my father worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What number is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 43. This is where my father worked and this is where I came most frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the remainder of the photographs? If you can recognise another place where you went, please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bottom photograph may also be relevant. It is around here somewhere that I saw these two men who had slaughtered a sheep and who were skinning it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, what was the last photograph's number? I didn't hear you say the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is photograph number 44, except you cannot see very well. I see some railroad cars there and I don't recall those at all. This is the road that leads out of the compound, and this is where a little concrete barrier was for stopping the railroad cars. And that's where they had slaughtered that sheep.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question: Mr. Delalic, testifying under oath, can you say with certainty on that day when there was this accidental discharge from the rifle of Mr. Delic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has not said the rifle of Mr. Delic at all --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already testified who was with you, so I'm not going to ask the question again. The Trial Chamber already knows what your answer was. After your return to Austria, did you, along with other members of your family who were there, continue to assist in the defence of Bosnia in the ways that you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, we redoubled our efforts, because after I returned to Bosnia, the HVO joined the Chetniks in attacking the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, I want to thank you for responding to our call and testifying here before this Tribunal. Your Honours, this completes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no cross-examination on behalf of Mr. Mucic. I would only make one request, that Mr. Mucic be allowed to use the restroom very quickly and he will be right back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, he may. Any questions? Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My name is Cynthia McMurrey and I represent Esad Landzo. Can you stand from your seat and see the Prosecution's model of Celebici in front of the witness stand? Do you see the concrete bunker that you were talking about that stopped the trains from going any further at the point near the administration building that you identified in the photographs? Can you point to that? I don't know if it's possible for you to point and identify this concrete block that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that where you said you saw, Smajo the butcher, slaughtering the sheep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you rise one more time? That concrete block that you see right there, that concrete block is really about one-quarter the size of the concrete block that is actually in Celebici, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose you're confusing him. You mean the replica he sees here?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll try to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That replica that you see here, that little piece that represents the concrete block, in actuality in Celebici, that concrete block is about four times larger than that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's much larger. It's like this maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. You can sit down now. You said that you saw one of the detainees with a knife with Smajo the butcher, I believe his name was Zeleni, when you were in the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On that occasion, together with Smajo, I saw one person whom I didn't know at the time, and he introduced him as Zeleni. He said he was a colleague from Bradina who also had a butcher shop in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you see any other detainees that you can remember when you were on your trip to Celebici, on your five or six trips in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only remember that man. As I was walking up and down that road going to see my father, most usually there would be no one there, maybe one or two guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you saw this detainee, Zeleni, did he look like he had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't look like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Questions by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Delalic. My name is Turone and I am going to ask you some questions for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, could you give us, please, the names of your brother and your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Semir Delalic and my father's name is Zahir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What was their job or their position in either Konjic or Prozor or anywhere in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, during the period we are talking about, did your brother live in Bosnia or did he also live abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, my brother was in Bosnia and he was a driver with the military police. It was at the time when I went to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And my father was working in one of the warehouses here, as I indicated on the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, sure. And exactly, your father, Zahir, which kind of warehouse had to take care of inside Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a military warehouse where weapons were stored, hand grenades, uniforms, military booths and military equipment in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And was your father, Zahir, part of Territorial Defence, either in Konjic or in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly what position did he have inside Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what his title exactly was, I don't know. He was simply there. He was in charge of receiving and issuing equipment. Several times when I was there, I saw lorries unloading or loading supplies and he was in charge of putting it all down on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he part of the Territorial Defence of Konjic or Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, he was a member of the Konjic Territorial Defence because he was in Konjic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And do you know who was his immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And what about your brother, you said he was a driver for the military police, who was the immediate superior of your brother Semir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that either too. Most of the time, we were together while I was there and I didn't see, I mean I didn't think that he had a major role to play there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Was it the MUP or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, he was a member of the military police, not the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say "military police", you mean military police of HVO or TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The TO military police because, at that time, there were already two different military polices because there were actually two armies. And at that time they were on the same side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, but your brother was a driver for the TO military police. And again, TO Konjic or TO Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Konjic. May I just add something? When I arrived in Prozor, the situation was calm and the town itself wouldn't have been exposed to any kind of problems if there hadn't been for the conflict between the HVO and Muslims later on. There were lines towards Kupres that were being held at that time and there was some shelling and this would have been all if it hadn't been for the conflict with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And most probably that was the reason why he came back to Konjic because nothing was actually happening in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you really have any questions for him for all that he has testified here? Do you really have any questions for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think I might have some questions for this witness. Why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be shown the -- this picture, please. It's exhibit -- Defence Exhibit D-13 A-1. Yes, this is a copy, the registrar might have the original, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It was tendered by Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In the meantime -- okay, this picture. Could you please see this picture and see whether you recognise yourself in this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And that's all with this picture, thank you. Could you tell us, who is Irfan? You have been talking about somebody by the name of Irfan. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Irfan married a cousin of mine and he was a driver and according to someone, he was also a bodyguard. Zejnil Delalic, well, he was a bodyguard, I don't know, but he definitely was a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay, you say that you arrived in Bosnia after your Uncle Sefik, end of July, how long did you remain in Bosnia entirely, in all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He's already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Konjic and how long did you stay in Prozor inside the one month and a half, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I stayed longer in Konjic. And since this is not very far, I mean the distance is 40 or 50 kilometres, it was possible for me to be both in Konjic and Prozor in one single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And when you arrived, you said that for two or three days you remained without a uniform and you were a civilian. Then, the first time you went to Celebici, you received a uniform and the rifle, taking them from the warehouse of your father, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: At that time, when you received this uniform and rifle, were you a member of TO already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean. I did not belong to Konjic or Prozor at the time, I simply put on an uniform and I made myself at their disposal. I made myself available to them, both to Prozor and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So, as a matter of fact, do you mean that you were considered a member of the TO by the headquarters of the TO, both in Konjic and Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. You became a soldier when you received a uniform --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, how can he know what other people think of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it might be easier to explain to the witness. You said you are commuting between Prozor and Konjic at all times. Now, when you became a soldier, when you got the uniform and you wore them, you were then a soldier, did you belong to Konjic or to Prozor, which of the groups did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I belonged to my hometown, to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any relationship also with the TO headquarters in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you simply received a uniform from the warehouse of your father, which was belonging to the TO headquarters of Konjic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was there, I didn't take any kind of oath to any of the staff. Therefore, when I went to Prozor, I simply took something that my father wanted to send to the staff. In Prozor, this was usually a certain amount of ammunition or things like that. I would often bring a piece of paper, so that they can receive it in an official manner at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But who gave you instructions then when you were in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What kind of instructions do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Well, any instructions of orders being, since you were in any case a soldier who was the person in charge of and entitled to giving you any kind of instruction or order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just said that I hadn't taken any oath to any of the headquarters, Konjic or Prozor alike, so I didn't have a commander.
